Home/Agriculture

Agriculture

Convert acres, hectares, yield, seed, fertilizer, irrigation, and application-rate units.

What agriculture conversions measure

Agriculture conversions cover four measurement families: land area (acres, hectares), weight (kilograms, pounds, tonnes), volume (liters, gallons), and application/yield rates that combine the two - such as bushels per acre, kilograms per hectare, or liters per hectare.

Common agricultural use

Land is measured in acres in the US and hectares in most other countries. Crop yields are commonly reported in bushels per acre domestically and tonnes per hectare internationally. Fertilizer, seed, and pesticide application rates, along with irrigation volumes, are typically expressed per unit of land area.

Choosing a unit

Match your application-rate or yield unit to the same area basis you use for land measurement - mixing acre-based and hectare-based figures in the same calculation is a common source of error. When comparing US and international data, convert land area first (acres to hectares), then convert the rate accordingly.

Popular Conversions

Acre to Hectare Kilograms per hectare to Pounds per acre Liters per hectare to US gallons per acre

About Agriculture Conversion

Agricultural unit conversions bring together the area, weight, and volume measurements used specifically in farming, land management, and crop production. Land is measured in acres in the US and hectares almost everywhere else, crop yields are reported in bushels per acre in the US and tonnes per hectare internationally, and seed, fertilizer, and feed quantities are measured in a mix of weight and volume units depending on the material and region. Because farming operates across both metric and imperial-using countries, converting between these systems is a routine part of international agricultural trade, research, and equipment specification.

Some agricultural units are unusually specific to the field: the bushel, for instance, is a volume-based unit historically used for grain that varies slightly in weight depending on the crop (a bushel of wheat weighs more than a bushel of oats, because bushel weight standards are set per crop by regulatory convention rather than a single universal density). This converter supports the core land, yield, and quantity units used in agriculture, acres, hectares, bushels, and common weight units, useful for comparing crop yields, converting field measurements, or working with international agricultural data and equipment.

Agricultural conversions matter increasingly as farming becomes a more globally connected industry: comparing crop yield data from research published internationally, evaluating farm equipment or seed specifications from another country, or simply understanding how a farm's acreage compares to an international counterpart all require moving comfortably between the acre-and-bushel system common in the US and the hectare-and-tonne system used almost everywhere else, a gap this converter is built to bridge for growers, students, and agricultural researchers alike.

Because agricultural yield conversions (like bushels per acre to tonnes per hectare) depend on the specific crop's standard bushel weight, it's important to use the conversion factor for the actual crop in question rather than a generic figure, since applying a wheat-specific factor to a corn yield, for example, would produce a meaningfully inaccurate result.

Quick Facts

  • Most used units
    • Acre

Common Agriculture Measurements

Agricultural conversions combine standard area units (like the acre and hectare) with weight and volume units used for crop yields, seed rates, and land measurement.

UnitSymbolEqual to
Acreac4,046.86 m² (0.404686 ha)
Hectareha10,000 m² (2.47105 acres)
Bushel (US, wheat)bu≈27.2155 kg (60 lb standard)
Bushel (US, corn)bu≈25.4012 kg (56 lb standard)
Metric ton per hectaret/haStandard international yield unit

Conversion Formulas

  • Acres to hectares: multiply by 0.404686
  • Hectares to acres: multiply by 2.47105
  • Bushels per acre to tonnes per hectare (wheat): multiply by 0.0673
  • Tonnes per hectare to bushels per acre (wheat): multiply by 14.87
  • Pounds to kilograms (for feed/seed): multiply by 0.453592

Practical Examples

  • A 160-acre farm equals about 64.75 hectares, since 160 × 0.404686 ≈ 64.75.
  • A wheat yield of 60 bushels per acre is about 4.04 tonnes per hectare, since 60 × 0.0673 ≈ 4.04.
  • A 50 kg bag of fertilizer covers roughly the same area whether specified in kg/ha or lb/acre once converted.
  • A 500-hectare estate equals about 1,235.5 acres, since 500 × 2.47105 ≈ 1,235.5.

Frequently asked questions

Why does a bushel's weight depend on the crop?

A bushel is technically a unit of volume (about 35.24 liters), but US agricultural trade standardized a specific weight-per-bushel figure for each individual grain type based on typical density, so a bushel of wheat (60 lb) weighs more than a bushel of oats (32 lb), even though both fill the same volume.

How do I convert a crop yield from bushels per acre to tonnes per hectare?

The conversion factor depends on the specific crop's standard bushel weight. For wheat, multiply bushels per acre by about 0.0673 to get tonnes per hectare; for corn, the factor is about 0.0628, since each crop has a different standard bushel weight.

Why is farmland measured in acres in the US but hectares elsewhere?

The acre is a traditional English unit of land measurement that the US retained after gaining independence, while most other countries adopted the metric hectare as part of broader metric system adoption in the 19th and 20th centuries.

What is the origin of the acre as a land unit?

The acre traces back to medieval England, originally defined as the amount of land a yoke of oxen could plow in one day, and it was later standardized to a fixed area of 43,560 square feet.

How many acres are in a hectare?

One hectare equals approximately 2.47105 acres, making a hectare noticeably larger than an acre, about two and a half times the size.

When Should I Use Each Agriculture Unit?

  • Acre — Used for land listings and field sizes across the US, UK, and much of the Commonwealth.
  • Hectare — Used almost everywhere else for land registries, farm subsidies, and international crop reports.
  • Bushel — Used in the US for grain, corn, and soybean trading volumes.
  • Tonnes per hectare — Used internationally to report crop yield in agronomy research and trade statistics.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌ Confusing hectares with acres (a hectare is about 2.47 acres, not equal to one).
  • ❌ Mixing metric tons with US short tons when pricing grain shipments.
  • ❌ Reporting yield per acre when the source data was measured per hectare, or vice versa.
  • ❌ Assuming a bushel is a fixed weight, when it actually varies by crop (a bushel of wheat and a bushel of oats weigh different amounts).
  • ❌ Ignoring moisture content adjustments when converting harvested weight to standardized yield figures.

History

The acre has roots in medieval England, originally defined as the amount of land a yoke of oxen could plow in a single day, which is why it was long and narrow rather than square. The hectare arrived much later, introduced in France in 1795 alongside the metric system, defined simply as 10,000 square meters to make land measurement consistent with the meter. The bushel is older still, tracing back to English and Roman dry-volume measures used for grain trade centuries before standardized weights existed. As farming became a global trade, these regional units persisted even as science moved toward SI, which is why a wheat shipment today might still be priced in bushels while the field it grew in is registered in hectares.

Why Convert Agriculture Units?

Farmers and agribusinesses constantly compare land sizes, yields, and input rates across countries that use different measurement traditions. A US grower researching European farming practices needs hectares translated into acres, and an international buyer pricing a harvest needs bushels converted into tonnes.
